blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html:
The log-rank test tests H₀: two (or more) groups have the same survival experience over the whole follow-up. At each event time it compares the observed number of events in each group (O) with the number expected (E) if H₀ were true, sums over event times, and forms

χ² = Σ over groups (O − E)²/E, on (number of groups − 1) degrees of freedom.

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html: Kaplan–Meier curves for two groups let you see a difference. The log-rank test asks whether it is larger than chance would produce. At every moment someone has the event, it asks: given who was at risk in each group right then, how many of these events should each group have had if the groups were alike? Too many events in one group, time after time, adds up to a large χ².

blocks.label: Derivation
blocks.html:
At event time tⱼ, nⱼ subjects are at risk, n₀ⱼ of them in group 0, and dⱼ events occur. Under H₀ each at-risk subject is equally likely to be among the dⱼ, so the expected number in group 0 is

E₀ⱼ = dⱼ × n₀ⱼ/nⱼ.

Sum over all event times: E₀ = Σ E₀ⱼ; O₀ is the total observed in group 0. For two groups, E₁ = total events − E₀. The statistic Σ(O − E)²/E has the same form as the goodness-of-fit χ² (recall §10.6.2), with df = 2 − 1 = 1 (Bland & Altman, 2004).

Software uses a slightly more exact version. The count in group 0 at tⱼ follows a hypergeometric distribution with variance Vⱼ = dⱼ(n₀ⱼ/nⱼ)(n₁ⱼ/nⱼ)(nⱼ − dⱼ)/(nⱼ − 1). With V = Σ Vⱼ, the statistic is χ² = (O₀ − E₀)²/V, also on 1 df. The two versions are usually close.

blocks.label: Worked Calculation
blocks.html:
The §14.7 cohort: 147 households without the community education intervention, 153 with it; 120 dropouts at 86 distinct event times. The first three event times:

Month tⱼ At risk, no intervention n₀ⱼ At risk, intervention n₁ⱼ Dropouts dⱼ (no int + int) E₀ⱼ = dⱼ × n₀ⱼ/nⱼ O₀ⱼ − E₀ⱼ
0.1 147 153 2 (1 + 1) 2 × 147/300 = 0.980 +0.020
0.3 146 152 1 (0 + 1) 1 × 146/298 = 0.490 −0.490
0.5 146 151 1 (1 + 0) 1 × 146/297 = 0.492 +0.508
… … … … … …
  1. Continuing through all 86 event times: no intervention O₀ = 70, E₀ = 55.95; intervention O₁ = 50, E₁ = 120 − 55.95 = 64.05.
  2. The no-intervention group had 14.05 more dropouts than expected; the intervention group 14.05 fewer.
  3. χ² = 14.05²/55.95 + 14.05²/64.05 = 3.53 + 3.08 = 6.61, df = 1, p = 0.010.
  4. Variance version: V = 29.75, χ² = 14.05²/29.75 = 6.63, p = 0.010.

The log-rank test shows the groups differ (p = 0.01). It does not say by how much: that needs a hazard ratio (§14.6.1).

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html: In the §14.7 cohort, 0.66 of intervention households and 0.51 of the others were still enrolled at 24 months (the curves are Figure 14.4 in §14.7). The worked calculation above shows that a gap this size would be unlikely if the groups truly had the same survival (p = 0.01).

blocks.label: In R (optional)
blocks.html:
library(survival)
co <- read.csv("data/cohort_dropout.csv")
survdiff(Surv(time_months, dropout) ~ intervention, data = co)
                 N Observed Expected (O-E)^2/E (O-E)^2/V
intervention=0 147       70       56      3.53      6.63
intervention=1 153       50       64      3.08      6.63

 Chisq= 6.6  on 1 degrees of freedom, p= 0.01

Observed and Expected are O and E from the worked calculation (E rounded to 56 and 64). The (O-E)^2/E column gives the two terms of the hand formula, 3.53 + 3.08 = 6.61. The (O-E)^2/V column is the variance version, 6.63, which is the Chisq R reports, with p = 0.01.

points.html: H₀: identical survival across the whole follow-up. Like ANOVA’s F (recall §9.5), it is an overall test.

It weights every event time equally. It “is most likely to detect a difference between groups when the risk of an event is consistently greater for one group than another” and is unlikely to do so “when survival curves cross” (Bland & Altman, 2004). Look at the curves as well as the p-value.
It gives a p-value only, no effect size and no confidence interval. It cannot adjust for covariates; Cox regression (§14.6) does both.
It plays the role of the t-test or Mann–Whitney test (recall §9.2.2 and §10.2) for censored time-to-event data, which neither of those can handle.

blocks.label: Checkpoint 14.2

questions.prompt: A Kaplan–Meier curve for Group A lies above Group B’s throughout follow-up, and the log-rank test gives p = 0.03. A colleague concludes: “Group A has a lower hazard at every single time point, guaranteed.” What is the overreach?
questions.answer: Two overreaches. First, S(t) is cumulative: a curve that stays higher reflects the sum of all hazard up to t. Group A can have a higher hazard than Group B during some periods and still keep a higher S(t), because of an advantage built up earlier; hazards can cross while survival curves do not. Second, the log-rank test is an overall test across the whole follow-up. p = 0.03 is evidence that the survival experiences differ overall, not a guarantee of anything at each time point, and nothing in statistics is “guaranteed”.

questions.prompt: A two-group log-rank analysis gives O = 30, E = 24 in Group A and O = 20, E = 26 in Group B. Compute Σ(O − E)²/E, its df and approximate p-value.
questions.answer: χ² = (30 − 24)²/24 + (20 − 26)²/26 = 36/24 + 36/26 = 1.500 + 1.385 = 2.88, df = 2 − 1 = 1. The 5% critical value for 1 df is 3.84, so p > 0.05; exactly, p ≈ 0.09. No convincing evidence that survival differs, though Group A had 6 more events than expected.

questions.prompt: Why can the log-rank test not tell you whether the intervention’s association with dropout remains after adjusting for household income?
questions.answer: The log-rank test compares groups defined by one categorical variable. It has no way to include a continuous covariate such as income, and it gives no effect size. Cox regression (§14.6) includes several predictors at once and gives an adjusted hazard ratio with a CI.
